title: Ivo and the Silence
premise: After her mother's funeral, Ines Yarrow returns to the decaying family house to prepare it for sale, cataloging the silences that defined their relationship. Behind a wardrobe she discovers a box of letters her mother wrote but never sent—letters that reveal a hidden love, a sacrificed life, and the reason for her lifelong coldness. As Ines reads them aloud to her estranged brother Tomas, the siblings confront how duty corrupted their mother's capacity for love, and whether they have inherited the same silence. The novel ends on the morning of the house sale: Ines finally says goodbye out loud in the empty hallway, sends one of the unsent letters at last, and walks out belonging—to herself—for the first time.
about_author: Oscar Oyelaran is a Nigerian-British writer who spent a decade as an archivist before turning to fiction, a career that taught him how much of a life lives in what was never said. He writes about inheritance, houses, and the families we fail to leave.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Three days after the funeral, Ines begins cataloging the house room by room for the estate agent, treating objects as evidence of a mother who never spoke plainly. She practices saying 'I loved you' to empty chairs and fails every time. Emotional beat: grief expressed as bureaucratic control.

chapters.title: Tomas Arrives
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Her brother Tomas appears unannounced, expecting to sign papers and leave within a day. Their exchange is all logistics and old grievances—their mother trained them both not to ask real questions. Emotional beat: sibling estrangement mirroring the maternal silence.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Moving the wardrobe in the master bedroom to check for damp, Ines finds a shoebox wedged against the wall: dozens of letters, addressed but never posted, spanning thirty years. Her hands shake too badly to open the first one. Emotional beat: discovery as intrusion—the dead speaking anyway.

chapters.title: Dear You
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, intercut with the first letter. The earliest letter, written at nineteen, is addressed only to 'You'—passionate, funny, alive, nothing like the woman Ines knew. Emotional beat: vertigo of realizing the mother was once a stranger.

chapters.title: What Tomas Won't Read
chapters.summary: Third person, alternating. Ines shows Tomas the box; he refuses, insisting some things should stay buried, then takes a letter anyway when he thinks she isn't looking. Emotional beat: duty versus curiosity, the family disease in miniature.

chapters.title: The Man in the Letters
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Through 1980s letters, a name emerges: Gabriel Osei, a musician her mother loved while engaged to Ines's father. The letters trace her choosing duty—and the exact moment her voice went quiet. Emotional beat: power of family expectation to corrupt love into silence.

chapters.title: Estate Agent Tuesday
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The agent values the house; a cash buyer looms, compressing time. Ines lies about being ready. That night she reads letters aloud alone, giving her mother the voice she never used. Emotional beat: deadline pressure sharpening the need to say goodbye properly.

chapters.title: Gabriel Is Alive
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas, unable to resist, tracks down Gabriel Osei through old gig listings—now a retired music teacher two towns away. He tells no one, sitting outside the man's house without knocking. Emotional beat: cowardice inherited, recognized with horror.

chapters.title: The Letter That Names Me
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A 1991 letter mentions 'the girl'—her own birth framed as another duty performed, yet followed by a paragraph of ferocious, wordless tenderness her mother could only write, never say. Emotional beat: love that existed, trapped behind duty.

chapters.title: Fight in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Third person. Tomas accuses Ines of exhuming their mother for her own absolution; Ines accuses him of hiding behind the sale like their mother hid behind propriety. Tomas leaves for a hotel. Emotional beat: rising tension—the silence reproducing itself in the next generation.

chapters.title: Letters to Father
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Later letters are addressed to her father after his death: confessions, apologies, an admission that she punished her children for her own unlived life. Ines understands her coldness had an author and a logic. Emotional beat: compassion replacing resentment.

chapters.title: The Knock
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas finally knocks on Gabriel Osei's door. Gabriel, calm and unsurprised, says he always knew the letters existed—he received one, once, decades ago, and returned it unopened out of respect for her marriage. Emotional beat: everyone chose silence; no one was forced alone.

chapters.title: One Delivered
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Gabriel visits the house, carrying the single returned letter, yellowed and sealed. He and Ines sit in the parlor; he does not open it, saying it belongs to the children now. Emotional beat: the past handing itself over gently, power dissolving into shared grief.

chapters.title: Contract Signed
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The buyer's solicitor calls: completion in ten days. Ines signs, then panics—ten days to finish reading forty years of letters and decide what goodbye means. Tomas returns, chastened, asking to read together. Emotional beat: clock ticking, reconciliation tentative.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Third person. Siblings read the letters aloud in shifts, alternating voices, laughing at the young mother's jokes, weeping at her restraint. The house fills with her silenced voice at last. Emotional beat: communion—the ritual they never had, built from paper.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The final letter, written weeks before death, is addressed to Ines and Tomas by name: unfinished, breaking off mid-sentence at 'what I should have told you was.' Emotional beat: climax approaching—the sentence left hanging becomes the novel's central wound.

chapters.title: Finishing the Sentence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Each sibling privately drafts what their mother would have said, and what they would say back. They cannot agree; each draft reveals more about the writer than the dead. Emotional beat: recognition that goodbye must be authored by the living.

chapters.title: Emptying Rooms
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Movers take the furniture; the wardrobe leaves a pale rectangle on the wall where the letters hid for thirty years. Ines keeps only the box and her mother's coat. Emotional beat: loss made physical, the house surrendering its secrets.

chapters.title: Night Before
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The last night in the house. Tomas confesses he almost burned the letters the day they were found; Ines admits she almost mailed them all to Gabriel to make the past his problem. They forgive each other in the dark. Emotional beat: honesty achieved at last, out loud.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Climax. Morning of completion, Ines stands in the empty hallway and speaks the goodbye she rehearsed for three years—naming her mother, naming the love, finishing the unfinished sentence in her own words while Tomas witnesses. Emotional beat: catharsis; the silence broken at its source.

chapters.title: Postage Due
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. At the post office, Ines mails the one returned letter onward to Gabriel with a note: 'She finished it this way. We thought you should have it.' Some letters, she decides, are meant to travel late. Emotional beat: release; duty transformed into gift.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.summary: Third person, closing. Weeks later, Ines writes the first letter of her own life—a real one, stamped and sent—and Tomas phones just to talk. Neither inherits the silence. Emotional beat: resolution; love chosen over duty, belonging found in speech.
